messages.body_plain:
Hi Mac,

You should use:

rmc.firstrow.header = c()
rmc.header.length =c()

because you do not have a file header, you only have column names which is not the same.

Further, rmc.nrow will be ignored by GGIR because this argument is only needed when interaction with function read.myacc.csv directly.

I just tested it on your file and for me this works now.

Best, Vincent

Hi, I just found this looking for how to resolve my own issue trying to run GGIR on some old awd files. messages.subject: Differentiating MVPA from off-road motorcycle transport
messages.subject_clean: Differentiating MVPA from off-road motorcycle transport
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I would be grateful if anyone has any suggestions that might help me. I have searched this group but I don't believe this question has been asked before.

I am about to start a study looking at 24-hour movement behaviour in Malawi. We will be measuring participant's activity over 7 days, using Axivity AX3 wrist-worn accelerometers on their dominant wrist. We plan to analyse the output using GGIR. We will be recording at 100Hz, with a range +/-8g. Currently using GGIR version 3.1.0 (I realise I need to update this).

However, our study is split across a rural and an urban site. In the rural site, particularly, the main form of motorised transport is by motorbike, on dirt tracks. I have been out with the field team on the back of one of their bikes while wearing an accelerometer, and when I processed the data with GGIR, I noticed on the 'file summary report' (which I've attached) that the period of time corresponding to me being on the motorbike (around 09:00 - 10:00am and 15:00 - 16:00 on Tuesday 25th June) seem to have been identified as moderate PA.

I wondered about reducing the sampling range, but on the same day I went for a run and the acceleration is similar or possibly even higher (between around 17:00 - 18:00 on the visual report).

Does anyone have any experience or suggestions of how to exclude or differentiate physical activity from motorcycle transport? My understanding is that travel by car is usually filtered out (presumably because of the smoother nature of the acceleration? - although I am not entirely sure how this is done.)

Many thanks!
Ben

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] sleep_efficiency calculation question
messages.body_plain:
> ... but sometimes in part 5 output, there is no sleep_efficiency calculation for certain days, even if the data is complete in the part 4 night summary output.

Part 2, 4 and 5 focus on a different time segment s and can have different inclusion criteria. This is why number of days, nights or windows reported can differ between these parts. Note that part 4 does not focus on days but on the nights.

For this reason, part 5 copies some of the part 4 variables to part 5 to ease comparing behaviour during sleep period time window with behaviour during day time waking hours.

Note that as of recently 'sleep_efficiency' in part 5 is no longer called as such but 'sleep_efficiency_after_onset' to better reflect what it is.

Best,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Hello David,

When I google the error message it brings me to the fread function in the data.table package (https://github.com/cran/data.table/blob/master/R/fread.R#L55-L56). This indicates that there is no data to be stored. I see you are trying to force GGIR to even consider files with 0MB with parameter minimumFileSizeMB = 0. So, that could be the problem: GGIR is not designed for handling recordings that have only a few minutes or no data. If you have a series of shorter recordings that together could form a continuous multi-day recording then consider parameter 'maxRecordingInterval' which allows you to append those recordings. Otherwise it seems best to skip the very short recordings.

Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Strange output regarding VPA (clipping?)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nina,

Did you talk to the participant and ask what they were doing during those hours?
If they cannot remember than ask whether they have occupations or hobbies that could also this? For example, endurance sport.

Further, it may be worth inspecting the raw data by using
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/read.gt3x/vignettes/batch_loading_gt3x.html
based on the read.gt3x. You could for example load the first 2 days and plot each individual axis of raw data.

If you see clear flat lines near the maximum acceleration values then that would indicate consistent clipping, but if so then it would be surprising that GGIR did not detect it. If you see more fluctuating signals then I think it is more likely that it is either:
True movement/vibrations
Malfunction of the accelerometer => Try to trace other recordings with the same device and see whether this patterns occurs in other recordings.

Best,
Vincent

In Nina's figure I find it suspicious that the z-acceleration is consistently above 2.5g: Not even a fraction of the data is low.

Nina reports back that this happened to ActiGraph and ask them to investigate and provide a clarification.

messages.subject: Imputation of non-wear time
messages.body_plain:
Dear GGIR group

I wonder if anyone has an answer to my question related to the imputation of non-wear time in GGIR. In one of our research projects, participants were asked to record the times when they removed the device and the associated reasons. We are interested in knowing whether it is possible to feed this information into GGIR by specifying the time segment(s) where we want GGIR-based imputation to be performed and those where we want them to be imputed by a specific intensity category.

For example, if we know that the device was removed from 9:00-9:30 for running, can we set this 30 minutes as MVPA? For other time segments detected as non-wear by the GGIR algorithm but not reported by participants in their log diary, we would still want the auto-imputation to be done. I know there is an option of using the TimeSegments2ZeroFile, but my understanding is that it only works with relabelling the non-wear/invalid segments as zero movement (e.g., when the participants did not wear the devices for sleep).

Thank you.

Best regards,
John.

messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,
Maybe I can add some hints from my experience.
I came across this error message at the same stage in pretty different scenarios using GGIR 3.1.2 on GENEActive devices in a 10-day or 21-day recording paradigm:

1) The raw data file may actually be corrupt at a certain point in the recording (one data page corrupted but previous and subsequent are ok). {GGIRread} seems to read only the first sequence of healthy pages until the corrupted page which may result in just a few hours with a high non-wear fraction and without a single clean night. This leads to the error message Jingfeng observed.  Solution: Some raw files can quickly (but carefully) be sanitzed by hand, by deleting the corrupted pages. (e.g., GENEActive software throws an informative error with the erronous page number, when attempting conversion to csv). The GGIR pipeline runs properly on the sanitized raw data, at least with the resulting data gaps of approx. 40 minutes I had so far. This can indeed save 21 days of valid data!

2) Vincent van Hees' response (HASPT.ignore.invalid = TRUE) above can indeed help in scenarios pictured by Jingfeng, when sleep periods and surrounding activity are still recorded.

3) Despite ignoring periods of invalid data, as in (2), this error still haunts me, when I have participants who wore a device maybe 1 hour in 21 days, and I attempt to produce the experimental part6 with these arguments:
GGIR(
  part = 1:6,
    do.report=c(2,4,5,6),
  # pretty standard configuration ...,
  save_ms5rawlevels = TRUE,
  cosinor = TRUE,
  part6CR = TRUE,
  part5_agg2_60seconds = TRUE,
  part6_threshold_combi = "30_100_400"
)
Avoiding part 6 may save the rest. Not sure which of the arguments is the breaking point. With the "graphperday_..." pdf still finishing, you can inspect and exclude such an unfortunate nonwear surprise.

4) Sometimes even avoiding part 6 doesn't help but avoiding part 5 does; at least for the sake of finishing the pipeline without errors. However, note another flag for big nonwear: part 4 does not have any results:
"report not stored, because no results available" Again, have a look at "graphperday... .pdf" to confirm big nonwear.

I understand that GGIR is meant for recordings with meaningfull data, but I see utility for more safety belts and more informative messages in the context of big nonwear-recordings.
Many thanks for the great software!
Konstantin

messages.subject_clean: Part4 error related to defaultGuiderOnset and possible solution
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues,

When processing our actigraphy data using GGIR, we noticed that a number of raw data files (about 15 out of 155) generated an error message during Part 4:
"Error in if (is.na <http://is.na>(defaultGuiderOnset) == TRUE) { : argument is of length zero”

After some investigation, we traced the error message back to function g.sib.det(). See below our processes and proposed solution:
The printed error message occurred in line 297 in g.part4.R
The issue is from the variable defaultGuiderOnset having a NULL value (which results in is.na <http://is.na>(defaultGuiderOnset) == TRUE to have length 0).
To find out why the variable defaultGuiderOnset is NULL, we noted that it takes its value from SPTE_start[j], as assigned on line 292.
SPTE_start came from the meta.sleep.folder, which contains RData outputs generated by function g.part3().
We compared the milestone 3 files from data files that ran successfully and files that failed and observed that in the data frame "sib.cla.sum," files that failed contained the value 0 in the night variable, while files that ran to completion had night indexes starting at 1.
We looked at the g.part3.R file to find out where the values for the variable night were generated.
The data frame "sib.cla.sum" is created by the function g.sib.sum() in line 118, and this function requires an input parameter "SLE."
SLE was generated using the function g.sib.det() in line 82.
>From here, we looked at g.sib.det.R.
The variable night is initialized in line 116 to contain the value of 0.
 These values were later modified according to another variable, sptei, which was initialized as 0 in line 221.
We believe the problem lies in lines 230 and 231, where nights containing data under 60 epochs were skipped, and the sptei was not updated in the next line (i.e., at this point, for these nights, sptei == 0).
It follows that, for nights under 60 epochs, the variable night will have a value of 0.
So, in g.part4.R, when the defaultGuiderOnset variable is set to SPTE_start[j], where “j” is the location index in the list nnights.list (line 265) and that a location index of 0 will result in NULL values, we know the following:
min(sib.cla.sum$night) == 0, for these problematic files
(lines 216-217) first_night = min(sib.cla.sum$night)
last_night = max(sib.cla.sum$night)
(line 219) nnightlist = first_night:last_night
(line 226) nnights.list = nnightlist
Since “j” will be of value 0 in the first iteration of the for-loop starting at line 265, we will see SPTE_start[j] == NULL, and consequently, defaultGuiderOnset == NULL.
In our specific cases, we can address this issue by running GGIR() separately for input data files that crashed due to this error by skipping their first night in part 4 (by adding the argument "excludefirst.part4 = TRUE" to GGIR()). However, for replicability purposes, it is not ideal that these input files will be run using a slightly different shell script than the rest of the inputs.

We wanted to share these with the rest of the GGIR community in case anyone else has run into a similar issue. If helpful, we would also like to propose a potential fix in the source code so that this won't be an issue for future projects:
In file g.sib.det.R OR g.sib.sum.R, whichever is more convenient and appropriate, consider implementing a change such that the final output is free of rows in which night is equal to 0.
Sample code: df <- df %>% filter(night !=0), where df is the name of the output data frame ("metatmp" or "sib.cla.sum," depending on where the change is implemented).
The reason why we think this fix might work is because the nights with night = 0 are, by design and reason of too little data, to be skipped. Therefore, dropping those rows should not be a major cause of concern.
We hope some of you might find this information helpful -- thanks!

Best,
Grace

> g.shell.GGIR(

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Creating advanced sleep log
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jess,

Correct, the advanced sleeplog is date oriented. So, it has the wakeup time and then the bedtime or sleeponset time for the following night. Note this is also the case if the person wakes up after midnight. In your example that would mean that even if the person fell asleep at 1am on 4/5/2024, the sleep diary would still be

date_d1, wakeup_d1, onset_d1
3/05/2024, 07:00, 01:00

Further, you can double check your assumptions by running GGIR and inspecting the guider estimates in the part4_nightsummary_sleep_full.csv because they should reflect the sleep diary for each night.

It would be great if you could suggest how we can improve the phrasing of https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/chapter9_SleepFundamentalsGuiders.html#guider-sleeplog I need to spread my attention to many aspects of GGIR and struggle a bit to optimise every detail, so any feedback will be much appreciated.

Best,

Vincent

messages.subject: incongruent data with 2 watches worn simultaneously
messages.subject_clean: incongruent data with 2 watches worn simultaneously
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Our team was interested in looking at the outputs from two watches worn at exactly the same times and set up the same way, so our PI wore two Geneactiv devices on the same wrist to see whether we would get congruent outputs after extracting the data from both and running them through GGIR.

The watches were set up the same way at 85.7 Hz. They were worn at same time. They were worn on the same wrist, one above the other, but not touching each other. We found that there were some discrepancies between the night summary data between the two watches. Most nights had similar sleep onset and wake times, which is what we would expect. However, nights 1 and 4 in particular showed larger discrepancies, with differences up to 3 hours. Please see attached screenshot of the Part 4 data for the two watches.

- Has anyone else ever experimented with wearing two watches at once?
- If so, did you find any differences in the recorded sleep data between the two devices?
- Does anyone have insight into why we would have such different data between the two devices, even when they were worn and taken off at the same time?

Thank you!
Ruth Bieber-Stanley, ASF team at CWRU

messages.body_plain:
We have never done such testing, so I can't share any of our own experiences.

Did you compare the signal plots between your recordings, like the graphperday (/meta/sleep.qc) or the file summary report (/results/file summary reports)? How do those compare, particular in the evenings and mornings? Do the sleep onset and wake up times all seem plausible/reasonable in isolation?

Were the devices worn continuously over the 5 days? Short-ish non-wear periods before or after sleep periods can sometimes be "missed" by GGIR, instead being considered as sustained inactivity bouts, which might lead to differences in the sleep onset and wake up detection. I have seen other instances where it seems like GGIR's "decisions" about things like non-wear, sleep onset, wake time, etc. can rest on a knife's edge, so to speak. In other words, very slight differences in the underlying signal may result in large discrepancies in the final outputs.

On Monday, July 29, 2024 at 11:38:47 AM UTC-4 Ruth Bieber-Stanley wrote:
> Hello,
>
> Our team was interested in looking at the outputs from two watches worn at exactly the same times and set up the same way, so our PI wore two Geneactiv devices on the same wrist to see whether we would get congruent outputs after extracting the data from both and running them through GGIR.
>
> The watches were set up the same way at 85.7 Hz. They were worn at same time. They were worn on the same wrist, one above the other, but not touching each other. We found that there were some discrepancies between the night summary data between the two watches. Most nights had similar sleep onset and wake times, which is what we would expect. However, nights 1 and 4 in particular showed larger discrepancies, with differences up to 3 hours. Please see attached screenshot of the Part 4 data for the two watches.
>
> - Has anyone else ever experimented with wearing two watches at once?
> - If so, did you find any differences in the recorded sleep data between the two devices?
> - Does anyone have insight into why we would have such different data between the two devices, even when they were worn and taken off at the same time?
>
> Thank you!
> Ruth Bieber-Stanley, ASF team at CWRU
